notes.3:5: The Greek text reads "cities of the Perizzites" (interpreting Hebrew perazi as a gentilic), whereas the Hebrew MT refers to unwalled towns.
notes.3:9: The Greek text reads "Phoenicians" and "Sanior" (vs. MT "Sidonians" and "Sirion"), and in v. 10 treats "Misor" (MT "the tableland") as a proper name and reads "Elcha" (MT "Salecah").
notes.3:12: The Greek text reads "we plundered" (epronomeusamen), where the Hebrew MT has "we took possession of"; in v. 11, "in the citadel" translates Hebrew "in Rabbah."
notes.3:14: The Greek text reads the distinct names "Arbok" (vs. "Argob" in vv. 4, 13), "Gartasei," "Homachathei," and "Bassemath" (corresponding to MT "Geshurites," "Maacathites," and "Bashan").
notes.3:17: "Machanareth" reflects a fusion of the Hebrew preposition with "Chinnereth," and "Ashdoth-pisgah" (Greek Asedoth) transliterates Hebrew "slopes of Pisgah."
notes.3:27: "The Hewn One" (Lelaxeumenou) renders the name "Pisgah" as a Greek participle; similarly, v. 25 reads "Antilebanon" (MT "Lebanon") and v. 26 reads "overlooked" (MT "was angry with").
notes.4:9: The Greek includes "on the day of the assembly" (absent in the Hebrew MT) and places the verse break mid-clause between the verb ("when ... said") and its subject ("the Lord") in v. 10, which English word order groups at the start of v. 10.
notes.4:20: This Greek text shifts from "you" to "us," repeats "out of Egypt," and translates the Hebrew "people of inheritance" with the adjective eukleron ("heritage" or "favored").
notes.4:34: Where the Hebrew MT has "great terrors," the Greek reads "great visions" (horamasin megalois, deriving the Hebrew from the root "to see"), and writes "our God" without "the Lord."
notes.4:47: The Greek text (following Codex Vaticanus) reads "Gog" where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "Og."
notes.4:48: The Greek text reads "Seon" (representing Hebrew Si'on, an alternate name for Mount Hermon, distinct from Mount Zion in Jerusalem).
notes.4:49: The Greek omits the Hebrew MT phrase "as far as the sea of the Arabah" and renders Hebrew "at the foot of the slopes of Pisgah" as "from Ashdoth the hewn" (apo Asedoth ten laxeuten), translating Pisgah etymologically as "hewn."
notes.5:14: The Greek text includes the creation rationale ("for in six days the Lord made both heaven and earth, and the sea, and all that is in them"), paralleling Exodus 20:11, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text omits this clause here.
notes.5:17: In the Greek manuscript tradition of Deuteronomy 5:17-18, some witnesses (including Codex Vaticanus/Swete) place adultery (v. 17) before murder (v. 18), while the Sixtine/Brenton order adopted here places murder (v. 17) before adultery (v. 18) and theft (v. 19); compare the distinct Septuagint order in Exodus 20:13-15 (adultery, theft, murder).
notes.5:29: "Who will grant" translates the literal Greek idiom τίς δώσει, reflecting a Hebrew expression of earnest wish ("Oh that...").
notes.5:33: "So that He may give you rest" translates the Greek καταπαύσῃ σε, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "so that you may live."
notes.6:4: The Greek text opens this verse with an introductory superscription ("And these are the statutes... out of the land of Egypt") not present in the Hebrew Masoretic Text, before introducing the Shema ("Hear, Israel: the Lord our God is one Lord").
notes.6:5: "Mind" translates the Greek διανοίας (compare Matthew 22:37; Mark 12:30), where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "heart."
notes.6:8: "Immovable" translates the Greek ἀσάλευτον (neuter singular, "fixed/unshaken"), where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has "frontlets/bands."
notes.6:16: "The Testing" translates the Greek place-name τῷ Πειρασμῷ, which renders the Hebrew name Massah by its meaning and creates a wordplay with the verb "test" (ἐκπειράζω).
notes.6:25: "Mercy" translates the Greek ἐλεημοσύνη ("mercy/compassion"), the Septuagint's rendering of the Hebrew term usually translated "righteousness."
notes.7:10: The Greek reads "those who hate" (τοῖς μισοῦσιν) twice without an explicit object ("Him"); "to their face" (κατὰ πρόσωπον) denotes direct, personal repayment.
notes.7:16: Where the Hebrew reads "all the peoples," the Greek reads "all the spoils of the nations" (πάντα τὰ σκῦλα τῶν ἐθνῶν); "stumbling block" translates σκῶλον (lit. a thorn or pointed stake).
notes.7:19: The Greek shifts to "the Lord our God" (where the Hebrew has "your God") and reads "uplifted arm" (βραχίονα τὸν ὑψηλόν) rather than "outstretched arm."
notes.7:21: The Greek reads "you will not be wounded" (οὐ τρωθήσῃ, from τιτρώσκω) where the Hebrew has "you shall not dread," and "mighty" (κραταιός) where the Hebrew has "awesome."
notes.7:24: The Greek reads "from the place of those people" (ἐκ τοῦ τόπου ἐκείνων, lit. "from the place of those ones") rather than the Hebrew "from under heaven," and has third-person singular "until He utterly destroys them" (as in v. 23).
notes.8:2: Unlike the Hebrew, the Greek omits "these forty years" here (placing "look, forty years" in v. 4) and uses a passive verb, "might be discerned" (διαγνωσθῇ).
notes.8:3: The Greek omits "which you did not know," supplies "word" (ῥήματι), and reads "through the mouth of God" (διὰ στόματος θεοῦ) rather than "of the Lord."
notes.8:4: The Greek adds the clause about sandals not wearing away, reads "your feet did not become calloused" (οὐκ ἐτυλώθησαν) rather than "your foot did not swell," and concludes with "look, forty years" (ἰδοὺ τεσσεράκοντα ἔτη).
notes.8:15: The Greek reads "biting serpent" (ὄφις δάκνων, for Hebrew "fiery serpent"), "thirst" (δίψα, for "thirsty ground"), and "a spring of water" (πηγὴν ὕδατος, for "water"); "sheer rock" renders πέτρας ἀκροτόμου.
notes.8:17: Greek δύναμις ("power," also in v. 18) renders a Hebrew term spanning both "power" and "wealth," and the Greek adds "great" (τὴν μεγάλην).
notes.9:12: The Greek verb is second person singular ("that you commanded them"), matching "your people whom you brought out," where the Hebrew text reads "which I commanded them."
notes.9:13: The Greek adds the Lord's introductory words "I have spoken to you once and twice, saying," before the quotation, a distinctive Septuagint reading absent from the Hebrew text.
notes.9:22: The Greek renders the three wilderness place names (Hebrew Taberah, Massah, and Kibroth-hattaavah) by their literal meanings: "the Burning," "the Testing," and "the Graves of Craving."
notes.9:24: The Greek passive verb literally reads "from the day He became known to you" (referring to the Lord), whereas the Hebrew text reads "from the day I knew you."
notes.9:26: The Greek addresses God as "Lord, King of the gods," where the Hebrew text reads "Lord GOD."
notes.10:2: The Greek reads the second-person verb "and you shall write" (addressing Moses), contrasting with v. 4 ("And He wrote") and with the Hebrew text and other Greek witnesses that read "and I will write."
notes.10:3: The Greek translates Hebrew "acacia wood" as "imperishable wood" (literally "non-decaying wood"), its standard Septuagint rendering for this timber.
notes.10:6: The Greek preserves the distinct place names "Beeroth of the sons of Jakim" and "Misadai" (Hebrew Beeroth Bene-jaakan and Moserah), and in v. 7 reads "Gadgad" and "Taibatha" (Hebrew Gudgodah and Jotbathah).
notes.10:16: The Greek renders the Hebrew idiom "the foreskin of your heart" directly as "the hardness of your heart."
notes.10:18: The Greek explicitly includes "the resident alien" alongside the orphan and the widow in the first clause, where the Hebrew text mentions only the fatherless and the widow.
notes.11:14: In vv. 13-15 the Greek keeps Moses speaking in the third person ("all the commandments," "He will give"), whereas the Hebrew MT shifts to God speaking in the first person ("My commandments," "I will give").
notes.11:16: Greek πλατυνθῇ ("be widened") renders the Hebrew verb in the sense of "be wide/enlarged" rather than "be enticed/deceived," and the Greek links the participles at the end of v. 15 directly to the warning here.
notes.11:18: Greek ἀσάλευτον literally means "immovable" or "unshakable," rendering Hebrew totafot ("frontlets").
notes.11:24: The Greek text names Anti-Lebanon (Ἀντιλιβάνου) rather than the Hebrew MT's "Lebanon," and adds "the great" before "river Euphrates."
notes.11:30: The Greek reads "in the land of Canaan, which dwells toward the west" (MT: "of the Canaanites who dwell in the Arabah"), spells Gilgal as "Golgol," and renders Hebrew "oaks of Moreh" as singular "the high oak."
notes.12:3: Compared with the Hebrew MT, the Greek reverses the verbs for sacred groves ("cut down") and carved images ("burn with fire"), and ends intransitively with "their name will perish."
notes.12:5: The Greek specifies "in one of your cities" (MT: "out of all your tribes"), and v. 6 follows a shorter Greek text mentioning only burnt offerings, pledged offerings (ὁμολογίας), and the firstborn of cattle and sheep.
notes.12:18: The Greek reads "the resident alien" (ὁ προσήλυτος) "in your cities," where the Hebrew MT has "the Levite who is within your gates."
notes.12:23: Greek ψυχή ("soul/life") here carries the sense "life"; the Greek also adds "its" before "blood" and states the prohibition passively ("the life shall not be eaten with the meat").
notes.12:27: The Greek text here is markedly shorter than the Hebrew MT, omitting the clauses concerning the altar and the pouring out of the blood of sacrifices.
notes.13:5: This Greek text omits the clauses about keeping God's commandments and serving Him that appear in the Hebrew Masoretic Text and some other Greek witnesses.
notes.13:6: The Greek uses masculine singular 'the wicked person' (ton poneron) rather than neuter 'the evil', and reads simply 'from slavery' without 'house of' (contrast v. 11).
notes.13:10: The Greek reads 'you shall surely report about him' (anangellon anangeleis), requiring formal denunciation, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads 'you shall surely kill him'.
notes.13:17: The Greek adverb pandemei ('with the whole people / publicly') renders the Hebrew term for a whole offering; earlier in vv. 14 and 16 the Greek also refers to 'their land' and 'that land' rather than 'city'.
notes.14:1: This Greek text omits the prohibition against cutting or gashing oneself for the dead found in the Hebrew Masoretic Text and some Greek witnesses.
notes.14:5: The Greek lists five wild animals rather than the seven in the Hebrew Masoretic Text, notably identifying the last animal as the giraffe (kamelopardalis).
notes.14:13: Verse 14 (the raven in the Hebrew Masoretic Text) is absent from this Greek text, and the Greek bird list in vv. 12-18 follows a distinctive order and identifications including swan, ibis, pelican, and purple gallinule.
notes.14:21: The Greek specifies 'a lamb' (arna) rather than 'a young goat' as in the Hebrew Masoretic Text, and uses the passive 'it shall be given'.
notes.14:26: This Greek text omits the list of purchasable items (cattle, sheep, wine, strong drink) and reads 'you and your son' rather than 'your household', continuing directly into v. 27 without 'you shall not forsake him'.
notes.15:7: The rare Greek verb apostergo ('turn away affection / cease to love') is used here instead of the Hebrew idiom 'harden your heart'.
notes.15:10: The Greek repeats the lending command from v. 8 ('you shall surely lend him a loan... according to what he lacks'), which does not appear in v. 10 of the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.15:18: The Greek reads "the annual wage" (ephetion misthon) rather than "double the wage" of the Hebrew Masoretic Text, and uses a plural passive participle ("when they are sent away free") encompassing both male and female servants.
notes.16:1: Greek ton mena ton neon ("the month of new produce") renders Hebrew Abib, and LXX uses the second-person verb "you came out of Egypt by night" rather than MT's "the Lord your God brought you out."
notes.16:7: LXX combines both "boil and roast" (hepseseis kai opteseis, harmonizing with Exod 12:8-9) where MT has only "boil/cook," and reads "your houses" (tous oikous sou) where MT has "your tents."
notes.16:8: LXX adds both "a festival" (heorte) and the exception clause "except whatever is to be done for a person" (lit. "for a soul," psyche, echoing Exod 12:16), neither of which appears in MT.
notes.16:18: Greek grammatoeisagogeis ("court clerks" or "recorders") is a Hellenistic administrative term used in the LXX to translate Hebrew shoterim ("officers").
notes.16:21: Greek alsos ("sacred grove") is the LXX rendering of Hebrew Asherah; LXX also frames the second clause as a separate prohibition ("you shall not make for yourself") rather than a relative clause modifying the altar as in MT.
notes.17:3: Greek tou kosmou tou ouranou ("the array of heaven") renders Hebrew "host of heaven," and LXX reads third-person "which He did not command" (ou prosetaxen) rather than MT's first-person "which I did not command."
notes.17:7: LXX reads masculine ton poneron ("the evil person," also in v. 12 and quoted in 1 Cor 5:13), where MT has the ambiguous "the evil."
notes.17:9: Following Codex Vaticanus, the Greek text mentions only "the judge" here (omitting the Levitical priests found in MT and other Greek witnesses), though the following verbs remain plural and the priest appears in v. 12.
notes.17:14: Throughout vv. 14-20, LXX uses archon ("ruler") and arche ("rule") rather than basileus ("king") and "throne/kingdom" as in MT.
notes.17:18: Greek to deuteronomion touto ("this second law") translates Hebrew mishneh hattorah hazzot ("a copy of this law") and is the source of the book's English title, Deuteronomy.
notes.18:5: LXX adds "before the Lord God" and "and to bless" (cf. Deut 10:8), and concludes with "among the sons of Israel" where MT reads "all the days" ("forever").
notes.18:8: The terse phrase "apart from the sale according to paternal family" (plen tes praseos tes kata patrian) is difficult in both Greek and Hebrew, generally referring to separate proceeds from the sale of ancestral family property.
notes.18:10: LXX renders "making pass through fire" as perikathairon ... en pyri ("purifying ... by fire"); the dative pharmakois ("with charms" or "with sorcerers") at the end of v. 10 links directly to "chants an incantation" in v. 11 (where other Greek manuscripts read nominative pharmakos, "a sorcerer").
notes.18:16: LXX reads "the Lord your God" (sou, the people addressing Moses) where MT has "the Lord my God."
notes.18:22: Greek ouk aphexesthe autou ("you shall not spare him" or "hold back from him") differs from MT's "you shall not be afraid of him."
notes.19:3: Greek στόχασαι literally means "measure out" or "survey" (distinct from the Hebrew "prepare"), fitting the division of the territory into three parts to keep the refuge cities accessible.
notes.19:4: "In the past" renders the literal Greek idiom "before yesterday and the third [day]" (likewise in 19:6), an expression meaning previously.
notes.19:6: "Kinsman-avenger of blood" translates Greek ὁ ἀγχιστεύων τοῦ αἵματος, literally "the one acting as next of kin for the blood" (plural in 19:12); "strike him fatally" renders the literal idiom "strike his life" (also in 19:11).
notes.19:17: The Greek text reads γνώσονται ("shall know"), matching Codex Vaticanus, where other Greek witnesses and the Hebrew read "shall stand."
notes.20:1: The Greek reads ἵππον καὶ ἀναβάτην ("horse and rider"), whereas the Hebrew has "horses and chariots."
notes.20:5: "Scribes" translates Greek γραμματεῖς (also in 20:8-9), which the Septuagint uses here for the Hebrew term denoting military officers or officials.
notes.20:16: Unlike the Hebrew, the Greek text does not repeat "only from the cities of these peoples" at the start of verse 16, linking "not from the cities of these nations" in 20:15 directly into this clause.
notes.20:19: The Greek reads σίδηρον ("iron") rather than "axe," and frames the rhetorical question literally as whether a tree in the field is a human being to enter the siegework from before you.
notes.21:1: "Someone struck down" (and "the person struck down" in 21:2, 3, 6) translates Greek τραυματίας, literally "wounded person," used in the Septuagint for someone fatally wounded or killed.
notes.21:4: "Rough ravine" renders φάραγγα τραχεῖαν (distinct from Hebrew interpretations of a perennial stream), and "hamstring" translates Greek νευροκοπέω (literally "cut the sinews," also in 21:6), where the Hebrew refers to breaking the heifer's neck.
notes.21:12: Here and in 21:13 the Greek uses second-person verbs ("you shall shave... trim... remove"), whereas the Hebrew places these actions in the third person ("she shall...").
notes.21:17: The Greek reads ἀρχὴ τέκνων αὐτοῦ ("the beginning of his children"), whereas the Hebrew has "the firstfruits of his vigor."
notes.22:1: The Septuagint consistently renders Hebrew shor ("ox") as moschos ("calf") in 22:1, 4, 10, and here includes "on the road" and "and return them to him" beyond the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.22:9: Greek diphoron literally means "double-yielding" (bearing two crops), translating Hebrew kilayim ("two kinds"); hagiasthē ("be consecrated") indicates forfeiture to the sanctuary.
notes.22:21: The Greek omits "of the house" after "her father" and "the men of her city" before "shall stone her" (both in the Hebrew MT), and uses masculine singular ton ponēron ("the evil person," echoed in 1 Cor 5:13) here and in 22:22, 24.
notes.22:29: The Septuagint uses the Greek silver coin didrachma ("fifty didrachmas of silver") here, whereas 22:19 uses the transliterated siklous ("one hundred shekels").
notes.23:1: In both the Greek and the Hebrew numbering chapter 23 begins with this verse (numbered 22:30 in another common versification, which counts 23:2-26 as 23:1-25).
notes.23:8: Greek Idoumaion ("Idumean") is the Septuagint's Greek designation corresponding to Hebrew "Edomite" (similarly, 23:5 reads "from Mesopotamia" where the Hebrew MT has "from Pethor of Aram-naharaim").
notes.23:11: Following Codex Vaticanus, the Greek text reads "he shall go out into the camp," reflecting an early scribal omission (parablepsis) of the clause "outside the camp, and he shall not enter" preserved in other witnesses and the Hebrew MT.
notes.23:18: The Septuagint renders the Hebrew's two prohibitions as four clauses, pairing prostitution terms (pornē / porneuōn) with Hellenistic mystery-cult initiation terms (telesphoros / teliskomenos).
notes.23:25: The Septuagint reverses the order of the standing-grain law (23:25) and the vineyard law (23:26) compared with the Hebrew MT, where the vineyard law comes first.
notes.24:3: The Greek text reads "and" (kai) rather than "or if" as in the Hebrew Masoretic Text and some Greek manuscripts, joining the second divorce and the second husband's death with a conjunctive link.
notes.24:10: The Greek text reads "and you go into his house" (kai eiseleuse) without a negative particle, treating the clause as part of the condition leading into v. 11's command to stand outside; the Hebrew Masoretic Text and other Greek manuscripts prohibit entering ("you shall not go into his house").
notes.24:13: Greek eleemosyne ("mercy" or "charitable deed") renders Hebrew tsedaqah ("righteousness").
notes.24:17: This Greek text ends after "a widow," and v. 18 begins directly with "because," lacking the prohibition against taking a widow's garment in pledge and the opening "and you shall remember" found in the Hebrew Masoretic Text and other Greek witnesses.
notes.25:1: The Greek text reads the neuter singular to dikaion ("what is right") rather than the masculine "the righteous person" found in the Hebrew Masoretic Text and some Greek manuscripts.
notes.25:2: Greek kathieis means "you must seat him" (contrasting with the Hebrew "make him lie down"), and this Greek text ends after "before them," omitting the additional clause on beating him in proportion to his offense found in the Hebrew Masoretic Text and other Greek witnesses.
notes.25:5: Greek sperma ("offspring") is gender-neutral rather than the Hebrew "son" (ben); similarly, v. 6 reads "the child" (to paidion) rather than "the firstborn."
notes.25:18: Greek epeinas means "you were hungry" rather than "faint" as in the Hebrew Masoretic Text, and anteste ("opposed") is stronger than the Hebrew "met."
notes.26:5: This Greek text reads third-person singular erei ("he will say") rather than second-person "you shall say" as in the Hebrew Masoretic Text, and translates the famous Hebrew phrase ("a wandering Aramean was my father") as "My father abandoned Syria" (Syrian apebalen ho pater mou).
notes.26:8: The Greek adds "He Himself with His great strength" and renders the Hebrew "great terror" as "great visions" (horamasin megalois), deriving the Hebrew noun from the root "to see" rather than "to fear."
notes.26:12: Greek to deuteron epidekaton ("the second tithe") differs from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "the year of the tithe."
notes.26:14: Greek ekarpousa ("I have offered," a sacrificial term) renders the Hebrew "removed/consumed," and the text repeats epekousa ("I have obeyed") where the Hebrew Masoretic Text and other Greek witnesses read "I have done."
notes.26:17: Greek heilou ("you have chosen") and heilato in v. 18 ("He has chosen") render a rare Hebrew causative form of amar ("say"), whose sense is debated.
notes.27:7: Greek "θυσίαν σωτηρίου" ("sacrifice of deliverance" or "salvation") is the Septuagint's standard rendering for the Hebrew peace or well-being offering. The Greek also places "there" after "sacrifice" and adds "and be filled" after "eat."
notes.27:15: Throughout vv. 15-26, the Greek translates the people's liturgical response with the optative "Γένοιτο" ("So be it") rather than transliterating Hebrew "Amen." In this verse, the Greek also reads "the people" (without "all") and "craftsmen" (plural).
notes.27:22: The Greek reads "a sister of his father or his mother" (i.e., an aunt), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "his sister, the daughter of his father or the daughter of his mother."
notes.27:23: The Greek reads "νύμφης" ("daughter-in-law") where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has "mother-in-law," and then includes an additional curse against lying with one's wife's sister.
notes.27:26: Unlike the Hebrew Masoretic Text, the Greek includes "every person" and "all" ("all the words") and renders the verb as "remain in" ("ἐμμένει ἐν") rather than "confirm," wording closely echoed in Galatians 3:10.
notes.28:5: Greek ἀποθῆκαι ("storehouses") and ἐνκαταλίμματα ("reserves," literally "things left over," also in v. 17) differ from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "basket" and "kneading bowl."
notes.28:7: Here and in the other covenant invocations of blessing and curse (vv. 8-9, 12-13, 20-22, 24-25, 27-28, 35-36), the Greek uses the volitive/optative mood ("May the Lord..."), contrasting with the future indicatives used for the resulting outcomes.
notes.28:25: The Greek reads ἐπισκοπήν ("visitation," in the sense of divine judgment or punishment) and διασπορά ("dispersion"), where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "defeated" and "a horror."
notes.28:28: The Greek text binds the first two afflictions into a single genitive phrase, παραπληξίᾳ ἀορασίας ("derangement of blindness"), rather than separating them with "and" as in the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("madness and blindness").
notes.28:32: Following the shorter Greek text (as in Codex Vaticanus), vv. 31-32 lack the clause about having no helper and sons and daughters being given to another nation; thus neuter plural αὐτά ("them") refers back to "your sheep" in v. 31, and σφακελίζοντες depicts eyes wasting away in anguish.
notes.28:36: Greek τοὺς ἄρχοντάς σου ("your rulers," plural) differs from the singular "your king" in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.28:48: The Greek text omits "in thirst and in nakedness" (present in the Hebrew Masoretic Text and some Greek witnesses) and reads κλοιὸν σιδηροῦν ("an iron collar" rather than "an iron yoke").
notes.28:55: Greek βασκανεῖ ... ὥστε δοῦναι lacks an explicit negative particle before the infinitive because βασκαίνω itself conveys grudgingly withholding ("begrudge ... so as not to give").
notes.28:65: Following Codex Vaticanus, the Greek reads καρδίαν ἑτέραν ἀπειθοῦσαν ("a different, disobedient heart"), differing from other Greek manuscripts ("a despondent heart") and the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("a trembling heart").
notes.28:69: The Saints Greek Critical Text numbers this verse 29:1 and the rest of the chapter 29:2-29. The English keeps the Saints.Bible verse slots (28:69 and 29:1-28) shared with the Hebrew and Latin editions, so Greek 29:n appears at 29:n-1 in this chapter.
notes.29:4: The Greek reads third-person 'He led,' aligning with Moses as narrator, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads first-person 'I led' (though v. 5 still shifts to divine first-person speech, 'I am the Lord your God').
notes.29:7: The Greek reads singular 'I gave' (Hebrew: 'we gave') and writes Gaddei, transliterating the Hebrew gentilic 'the Gadite,' paired here with the tribal name Reuben.
notes.29:17: The Greek 'a root sprouting upward in gall and bitterness' differs from the Hebrew 'a root bearing poison and wormwood' and is closely echoed in Hebrews 12:15.
notes.29:18: Greek hosia moi genoito ('May holy things be mine') renders Hebrew 'I shall have peace,' and the closing purpose clause ('so that the sinner may not destroy the sinless along with himself') diverges markedly from the Hebrew idiom 'to sweep away the watered with the dry.'
notes.29:28: The Greek uses second-person plural pronouns throughout ('your God ... to you and to your children'), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads first-person plural ('our God ... to us and to our sons').
notes.30:3: The Greek reads "the Lord will heal your sins" where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "the Lord your God will restore your fortunes" (or "return your captivity").
notes.30:6: The Greek reads 'the Lord will thoroughly cleanse your heart,' interpreting the metaphor where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads 'will circumcise your heart.'
notes.30:14: The Greek adds 'and in your hands' after 'in your mouth and in your heart,' a phrase absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text and from Paul's quotation in Romans 10:8.
notes.30:20: The Greek uses the neuter pronoun 'this' (referring to loving, listening to, and holding fast to the Lord), whereas the Hebrew pronoun can be read either as 'He is your life' or 'that is your life.'
notes.31:1: The Greek reads "Moses finished speaking" (συνετέλεσεν Μωυσῆς λαλῶν), aligning with the Dead Sea Scrolls manuscript 1QDeut-b rather than the Masoretic Hebrew "Moses went and spoke."
notes.31:6: The Greek includes both "with you" and "among you" (μεθ᾽ ὑμῶν ἐν ὑμῖν), a distinctive Codex Vaticanus doublet, and lists three verbs of fear where the Hebrew has two.
notes.31:21: The Greek opens directly with the song standing in opposition as a witness, without the opening temporal clause ("when many evils and troubles have come upon them") found in the Masoretic Hebrew, and renders the people's "inclination" as "wickedness" (πονηρίαν).
notes.31:23: With third-person phrasing ("that the Lord swore to them, and He will be with you"), the Greek continues Moses from v. 22 as the speaker commissioning Joshua, whereas the Masoretic Hebrew attributes this verse to the Lord speaking in the first person.
notes.31:29: The Greek source text reads the verbless phrase "the evils at the end of the days" (τὰ κακὰ ἔσχατον τῶν ἡμερῶν), lacking "and [evils] will befall you" found in other Greek witnesses and the Hebrew—likely an early scribal eye-skip between two occurrences of ὑμῖν ("you").
notes.32:8: The Greek text reads "according to the number of the angels of God," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text has "sons of Israel" and a Dead Sea Scrolls manuscript (4QDeut j) reads "sons of God."
notes.32:23: Translates the Greek reading συνπολεμήσω ("wage war with," as in Codex Vaticanus), rather than συντελέσω ("spend / use up") found in other Greek manuscripts and corresponding to the Hebrew.
notes.32:43: The Greek preserves an expanded poetic conclusion calling on the heavens, the sons of God, the nations, and all the angels of God to rejoice and worship Him (clauses cited in Rom 15:10 and Heb 1:6).
notes.32:49: The Greek text (as in Codex Vaticanus) locates Mount Nebo "in the land of Canaan," whereas other Greek manuscripts and the Hebrew text read "in the land of Moab."
notes.32:51: "Contention" translates the Greek place name Ἀντιλογίας (lit. "contradiction" or "dispute"), the Septuagint rendering of Hebrew Meribah.
notes.33:2: Greek reads "Kadesh" (transliterating the Hebrew word for "holy ones") and "angels with Him" where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has a difficult phrase, read as "a fiery law for them."
notes.33:5: "The beloved one" translates the Septuagint rendering of the poetic name Jeshurun for Israel (also in 33:26), and Greek reads "ruler" rather than "king."
notes.33:8: Greek renders Hebrew Urim and Thummim as "manifestations" and "truth," and translates the place names Massah and Meribah as "Testing" and "Contention."
notes.33:10: Greek translates the Hebrew word meaning either "nostrils" or "anger" as "in Your wrath" and renders the term for "whole burnt offering" as "continually."
notes.33:17: Greek monokerotos ("unicorn," literally "one-horned animal") is the Septuagint rendering of the Hebrew term for a wild ox.
notes.34:1: Greek transliterates Hebrew arboth ("plains") directly as "Araboth" (also in 34:8).
notes.34:6: Greek has a plural verb ("they buried him") rather than the Hebrew singular ("He buried him") and transliterates Hebrew "the valley" as the proper name "Gai."
notes.34:7: This Greek text omits "his cheeks" (present in some Septuagint manuscripts), making "his eyes" the subject of "nor did they decay" (Hebrew: "nor had his vigor fled").
notes.34:11: Greek uses a masculine singular relative pronoun referring to Moses ("he whom the Lord sent to do them") rather than a neuter relative referring to the signs and wonders.
